# Deep Gaussian Processes for Financial Risk Modeling

Gaussian processes are well-established Bayesian non-parametric models for regression and classification, and GP-based recurrent extensions have also been used for time-series modelling [@rasmussen_gaussian_2008; @williams_gaussian_1995; @mattos_recurrent_2016]. Deep Gaussian processes extend this framework by composing multiple GP layers, giving a more expressive probabilistic model while retaining an explicit treatment of predictive uncertainty [@damianou_deep_2013; @salimbeni_doubly_2017].

In finance, GP-based methods have been applied to credit-risk and credit-rating problems [@mahajan_gaussian_2022; @huang_using_2011], volatility forecasting [@munoz-gonzalez_laplace_2014], algorithmic trading strategy identification [@yang_gaussian_2015], and market-risk approximation for trading portfolios [@lehdili_performance-enhancing_2025]. Basel III and the wider Basel Framework make banks' capital requirements explicitly risk-sensitive, so reliable estimates of probability of default (PD) and other loss-related quantities are important for both regulatory compliance and internal risk management [@basel_committee_basel_2011]. Against that background, comparing GPs and DGPs for credit-risk prediction is well motivated. At the same time, the finance literature cited above is still dominated by standard GP variants, with direct DGP applications appearing much less common. This section therefore compares GPs and DGPs with standard machine learning baselines on financial datasets, focusing on both predictive performance and the quality of uncertainty quantification, while also considering computational cost and interpretability.
